title: Chapter 14 — The Trade Of Literature
paragraphs: Democracy not only instills a taste for letters among the trading classes, but introduces a trading spirit into literature itself. In aristocracies, readers are fastidious and few; in democracies, they are far more numerous and far less difficult to please. The consequence is that among aristocratic nations, no one can hope to succeed without immense exertions — exertions that may bestow a great deal of fame but can never earn much money. Among democratic nations, by contrast, a writer may flatter himself that he will obtain at little cost a modest reputation and a large fortune. For this purpose he need not be admired; it is enough that he be liked. The ever-growing crowd of readers, and their continual craving for something new, ensures the sale of books that nobody much esteems.

In democratic periods the public frequently treats authors as kings treat their courtiers: they enrich them, and they despise them. What more do the venal souls born in courts, or worthy to live there, require? Democratic literature is always infested with a tribe of writers who look upon letters as a mere trade; and for every few great authors who adorn it, you may count thousands of idea-mongers.
